A dominant-control analysis further reveals distinct regional patterns in which topography, surface water, soil moisture, or vegetation serves as the leading control. Topography dominates about 68% of land, surface water and vegetation each about 14%, and soil moisture about 4%. These results provide a physically meaningful account of where and why land DDM coherence varies, together with an interpretable empirical basis for understanding how land-surface conditions influence DDM coherence and for informing the design of future GNSS-R land applications.

title: Robust real-time GNSS satellite clock estimation using atomic clock models with anomaly detection and mitigation
abstract: Abstract Real-time Precise Point Positioning (RT-PPP) relies heavily on precise Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) satellite clock products. Model-based clock estimation can exploit the improved stability of modern atomic clocks to establish and maintain a stable network timescale. However, conventional clock models cannot adequately handle clock anomalies, such as phase and frequency jumps, which can degrade clock estimation accuracy and compromise filter stability. To address this issue, we propose and validate an anomaly-aware real-time satellite clock estimation framework that integrates atomic clock modeling with anomaly identification, isolation, and recovery within a network solution, thereby limiting the propagation of clock anomalies into the network time reference. To further assess the reliability and practical applicability of the framework, the anomaly-confirmation parameters are systematically evaluated, and the computational efficiency is assessed to verify real-time feasibility. Subsequently, validation using actual GNSS data demonstrates the effective identification and mitigation of phase jumps, frequency jumps, and complex anomalies. Real-time service performance evaluation shows that the method achieves comparable or improved clock accuracy across multiple GNSS constellations, while significantly enhancing timescale stability. The proposed approach therefore provides a more stable and resilient real-time GNSS timescale, thereby supporting high-accuracy timing applications.

title: A method for monitoring aircraft height above ground across diverse landforms using GNSS reflected signals: a field study
abstract: Abstract Altitude above Ground Level (AGL) is an important parameter in aircraft flight operations and safety. Conventional aircraft altitude measurement techniques are largely constrained by their dependence on active signal transmission, sensitivity to environmental conditions, limited operational coverage, and inherently localized single-point measurement geometry. This paper presents a method that leverages Global Navigation Satellite System-Reflectometry (GNSS-R) to acquire AGL height, providing a complementary solution to current measurement systems. The proposed system employs an upward-Right-Hand Circular Polarization (RHCP) antenna and a downward-Left-Hand Circular Polarization (LHCP) antenna together with an Intermediate Frequency (IF) collector for raw data collection. The collected data are subsequently processed offline using a Software Defined Receiver (SDR). This paper proposes the Short‑Time Shortest‑Path (STSP) method to retrieve high‑accuracy GNSS‑R AGL, which uses only 25 incoherent accumulations and selects the shortest path delay when the reflected waveform exhibits multiple peaks. For a feasibility assessment, we installed the system on an Aurora SA60L aircraft and conducted an approximately 288-km flight from Dongying City to Tai’an City of Shandong Province, China. Dual-frequency Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) IF data on the shared frequency bands were collected during the flight over diverse terrains, including rural, urban, suburban, and mountainous areas. BeiDou Navigation Satellite System (BDS) B1C/B2a, Global Positioning System (GPS)/Quasi-Zenith Satellite System (QZSS) L1 C/A/L5, and Galileo E1C/E5a signals were leveraged to compute the code- level path -delay differences between direct and reflected signals. The measurements were used to retrieve the aircraft's heights above multiple distinct specular reflection points. The results demonstrate the capability of GNSS-R technology to obtain reliable AGL height estimates under various surface conditions. The GNSS-R derived AGL solutions were compared with the GNSS-Digital Elevation Model (DEM) for accuracy assessment. The results show that the proposed method achieves a height estimation accuracy of better than 4 m in flat terrain and about 15 m in mountainous areas.

title: A robust visual localization framework for UAVs using a zero-shot aerial-satellite image matcher and a particle filter
abstract: Abstract Positioning of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) normally relies on the Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS). However, GNSS signals are prone to blockage, interference, and spoofing, which can cause positioning failures and severely degrade mission performance. Aerial-satellite image matching using intelligent methods (e.g., deep neural networks) has emerged as a promising approach for achieving meter-level absolute positioning accuracy in GNSS-denied environments. To advance localization based on aerial-satellite image matching, we propose a robust localization framework that integrates a zero-shot aerial-satellite image matcher, termed the Generalizable Image Matcher (GIM), with a particle filter. First, the front-end visual odometry estimates the UAV trajectory from consecutive onboard images to produce an initial pose. Next, guided by the front-end estimate, candidate locations are sampled to crop the corresponding satellite sub-images. GIM is then used to match aerial and satellite images and infer absolute location cues. Finally, an adaptive weighting function is designed to fuse the front-end and back-end localization information, thereby yielding the final positioning result. Experiments were conducted using data collected along 12 flight trajectories spanning rural, urban, and farmland scenarios. Assuming that the initial position of each trajectory is known, the proposed method achieved an overall average positioning error of 5.02 m across all 12 trajectories, with average errors of 5.46 m for the nine real-data trajectories and 3.69 m for the three synthetic-data trajectories. Across the evaluated trajectories, which covered a cumulative flight distance of 104,566 m, no accumulation of positioning drift was observed. These results indicate stable positioning performance under the outdoor datasets and experimental conditions evaluated in this study.
